title: Notes on remembering what you read
author: Example author

blocks.text: Most of what we read is gone within days. This isn’t a flaw of attention: memory keeps what gets used and lets the rest fade.
The practical consequence is simple. Reading once is collecting; remembering starts when you come back to the material.
Forgetting is the default. Remembering is something you do on purpose.
A second look is worth most just before the memory fades. Too early and it adds little; too late and you are reading from scratch.
A rough schedule
The next day.
After three or four days.
After two weeks.
After a couple of months.
A starting point, not a rule: stretch the gaps for what you know well and shorten them for what keeps slipping.
A page covered in colour says nothing. A highlight is useful when it marks a choice: this sentence, and not the ten around it.
Try one colour for the main claims, one for examples and one for doubts. Three are enough; more turn the page back into noise.
Highlights are fragments. A diagram forces you to say how the fragments relate: what causes what, what is an instance of what.
If you can’t draw an arrow between two highlights, ask whether you really understood one of them.
A chapter diagram that needs scrolling is a second copy of the chapter. Aim for something you can read at a glance.
If the diagram is as long as the text, it isn’t a diagram yet.
Rereading feels productive because the text looks familiar. Familiar isn’t the same as remembered.
Close the book and rebuild the diagram from memory. The gaps you find are the parts worth a second look.
Explaining a chapter to someone else, even an imaginary listener, shows quickly where the explanation runs out.
Start from the main question of the chapter.
Give one example for each claim.
Say what would change your mind.
